lead: The air in a cylinder is never still. The inlet port, the valve and the piston set up organised, large-scale motions: swirl, a rotation about the cylinder axis; tumble, a rotation about an axis across the cylinder; and squish, a radial inward flow as the piston nears the head at TDC. Near TDC these motions break down into turbulence. In a CI engine they mix the injected fuel with air; in an SI engine they wrinkle the flame front and speed up the burn. The swirl ratio puts a number on swirl.
prereq: You need: flame speed and turbulence (flame velocity), and CI mixture formation (CI combustion).

blocks.text: A CI engine has only about 1 to 2 ms to mix its fuel with air, and the fuel arrives as a few narrow sprays into a chamber full of air. Unless the air moves past the sprays, each plume uses up the oxygen around it and the rest of the air is wasted: power falls and smoke rises. An SI engine has a ready-mixed charge, but a flame in still gas creeps at well under 1 m/s; turbulence raises the burning speed several times, so the charge burns in time, cycles vary less and the engine tolerates leaner mixtures and more EGR.

Organised motion and turbulence are different things. Swirl, tumble and squish are bulk flows with a clear direction. Turbulence is the small, random eddies that actually wrinkle a flame and mix fuel at the smallest scales. The organised flows store kinetic energy during the intake stroke and release it as turbulence near TDC, just when combustion needs it. Some syllabi list "swirl, squish and turbulence" together for this reason.

Swirl is rotation of the charge about the cylinder axis. It is produced during intake by the port and valve: a directed port that aims the flow at the cylinder wall, a helical port that spins the flow before it reaches the valve, or a shrouded (masked) valve that lets air enter on one side only. A shroud is simple but cuts the flow area, so volumetric efficiency suffers; helical ports are the usual choice.

Swirl persists through compression, losing some energy to wall friction. In a diesel with a bowl in the piston, the air is pushed into the bowl near TDC. Its angular momentum is roughly conserved while its radius shrinks, so it spins faster, like a skater pulling in their arms. For solid-body rotation the ideal gain is (bore ÷ bowl diameter)². Real gains are smaller because of friction and because not all the air enters the bowl. Too much swirl blows one spray plume onto the next, raises heat loss to the walls and costs volumetric efficiency.

Squish is the radial inward flow created when the piston crown comes very close to a flat part of the head, the squish band or squish area, near TDC. The gas in that thin gap is squeezed out towards the bowl or the centre of the chamber. It is strongest in the last 10° or so before TDC, when the gap is smallest (about 1 mm in a diesel). Squish is not a rotation; it is a squeezing flow that adds turbulence exactly at TDC. After TDC it reverses as reverse squish.

Tumble is rotation about an axis at right angles to the cylinder axis, so the charge rolls over like a barrel. A steep, straight inlet port in a four-valve pent-roof head produces it. As the piston rises, the tumble vortex is squashed into an ever flatter shape until it breaks up near TDC into intense turbulence. That is why modern petrol engines favour tumble: its energy arrives at the spark. The tumble ratio is defined like the swirl ratio, as the rotational speed of the tumble vortex ÷ engine speed.

In short: diesels rely mainly on swirl and squish; petrol engines mainly on tumble and squish. All three end as turbulence, and the right amount is a balance between faster mixing and burning on one side, and heat loss and lost breathing on the other (see combustion chambers).

examples.question: A DI diesel (bore 100 mm, stroke 110 mm) runs at 2000 rev/min with an in-cylinder swirl ratio of 2.2. Its piston bowl is 60 mm in diameter. Find (a) the swirl speed, (b) the tangential air velocity at the cylinder wall, (c) the mean piston speed and compare, and (d) the ideal swirl ratio in the bowl at TDC.
steps: (b) Angular speed ω = 2π × 4400 ÷ 60 = 460.8 rad/s. At the wall, r = 0.050 m: v = ω r = 460.8 × 0.050 = 23.0 m/s.
(c) Mean piston speed = 2 L N ÷ 60 = 2 × 0.110 × 2000 ÷ 60 = 7.33 m/s. The swirl at the wall moves about 3.1 times faster than the average piston.
(d) Ideal gain from angular momentum: (bore ÷ bowl)² = (100 ÷ 60)² = 2.78. Ideal bowl swirl ratio = 2.2 × 2.78 = 6.1.
Check: the gain is an upper bound; friction and the air left in the squish gap make the real bowl swirl ratio lower.
examples.answer: (a) 4400 rev/min. (b) 23.0 m/s at the wall. (c) 7.33 m/s, so the air sweeps the sprays about three times faster than the piston moves. (d) Ideally about 6.1 in the bowl, less in practice.

traps: Squish is a radial inward flow near TDC, not a rotation; swirl and tumble are rotations.
Swirl rotates about the cylinder axis; tumble rotates about an axis across the cylinder. Do not swap the axes.
The swirl ratio has no unit: both speeds are in rev/min (or both in rad/s).
Organised motion is not turbulence; it decays into turbulence near TDC.
More swirl is not always better: it raises heat loss, can overlap the spray plumes and cuts volumetric efficiency.

quiz.q: Define swirl, squish and tumble in one line each.
quiz.a: Swirl: rotation about the cylinder axis. Squish: radial inward flow from the squish band as the piston nears TDC. Tumble: rotation about an axis at right angles to the cylinder axis.

quiz.q: Name three ways of producing swirl.
quiz.a: A directed (tangential) port, a helical port and a shrouded (masked) inlet valve.

quiz.q: Why does swirl speed up when air is pushed into a piston bowl?
quiz.a: Its angular momentum is roughly conserved while its radius shrinks, so its angular speed rises, ideally by (bore ÷ bowl diameter)².

quiz.q: Why do modern petrol engines prefer tumble to swirl?
quiz.a: The tumble vortex is squashed by the rising piston and breaks into turbulence near TDC, just when the flame needs it, raising burning speed and cutting cycle-to-cycle variation.

quiz.q: An engine runs at 3000 rev/min with a swirl ratio of 1.8. Find the swirl speed.
Bore 90 mm, bowl 50 mm, in-cylinder swirl ratio 2.0. Find the ideal bowl swirl ratio.
Two DI diesels have swirl ratios 3.0 and 1.5 at the same speed and injection system. Compare mixing, smoke and heat loss.
quiz.a: The higher-swirl engine mixes faster, so the mixing-controlled stage is shorter and smoke lower, but heat loss and pumping loss are higher and plumes may overlap. The lower-swirl engine needs more spray holes and higher injection pressure to mix as well.

beyond: Engine developers measure swirl and tumble on steady-flow rigs and simulate them with CFD before casting a head; particle image velocimetry in optical engines shows the vortex breaking up. Some engines switch charge motion with valves in the port, high at low load and low at full load. Search for swirl ratio measurement, tumble flaps and in-cylinder PIV.

spec.aria: Three panels. Swirl, top view: a 100 millimetre bore with curved arrows round the axis and a 60 millimetre bowl; swirl ratio 2.2, 4400 revolutions per minute, 23 metres per second at the wall. Squish, side view: a piston with a bowl close under the head; arrows push gas from the 1 millimetre gap inward and down into the bowl. Tumble, side view: a pent-roof cylinder with a loop turning about a horizontal axis.
